newsitem.title: USA: Clinton takes wary stance on tobacco settlement.
newsitem.headline: Clinton takes wary stance on tobacco settlement.

text.p: President Bill Clinton reserved judgment on an agreement between the U.S. states and the tobacco industry on Friday, saying the administration would study it for several weeks to see if it met U.S. public health interests.

Earlier, tobacco companies agreed to pay out $368.5 billion, admit that tobacco is addictive and accept extensive federal regulation over their products and advertising as part of a landmark agreement with the U.S. states.
In return, the companies would get immunity from further punitive liability for any past deception, fraud or conspiracy.

"We must judge this agreement on whether it advances the public health and if it will reduce the number of children smoking cigarettes," said Clinton, who is attending the Group of Seven industrial nations summit in Denver. "The money, of
course, is an enormous amount of money," Clinton said.
He added that he wanted to focus on two aspects of the deal: the Food and Drug Administration's ability to regulate nicotine and the payment and distribution of the money.

In a separate written statement, Clinton directed his chief domestic policy adviser Bruce Reed and Secretary of Health and Human Services Donna Shalala to consult public health officials and others and to subject the pact "to the strictest scrutiny."
"We must now carefully consider whether approving this proposed settlement will protect the public health -- and particularly our children's health -- to the greatest extent possible," Clinton said.
"Protecting the health of the public and these children will be our measure of this proposed agreement."

White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters that he expected the evaluation of the deal to take "a matter of weeks, not months." Other U.S. officials said the two aides have been given four to six weeks to conduct the review.
The settlment will require legislation to put it into effect and the president's support is seen as crucial to its passage.
In August, 1995, Clinton authorized the FDA to regulate how cigarettes are sold and marketed in a bid to curb smoking among children.

The move defied conventional political wisdom, which predicted he would pay a heavy price in the 1996 presidential campaign. Instead, the move proved popular with voters and pushed the battle further into the political arena.

However, the issue is still very sensitive politically, particularly if the tobacco companies are seen to be getting off too lightly or if there is a public backlash against them being spared future punitive damages.
McCurry said that the specific aspect of the agreement limiting punitive damages was not in itself an obstacle to the White House.
"The limitation on punitive damages for past misconduct is not necessarily a deal-breaker for us," he said.

"We understand that the attorneys general extracted substantial concessions from the tobacco companies for this limitation and we'll evaluate whether the agreement as a whole advances the nation's public health interests," he added.
